claim: MessagePack attributes on T are ignored. Without a surrogate, the collector always takes the contractless path over every public read-write member. It never reads [MessagePackObject], [Key] or [IgnoreMember] on T, nor [DataContract], [DataMember] or [IgnoreDataMember]. The acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured' is therefore not met. For example, a member marked [IgnoreMember] on T is still serialized, and [Key(0)] int keys become string keys.

claim: The change includes an unrelated runtime edit to the timestamp writer. The timestamp32 check now tests the LOW 32 bits of data64 instead of the high 32 bits. Two consequences follow. Ordinary DateTimes with zero nanoseconds now take the 10-byte timestamp64 form instead of the 6-byte timestamp32 form, which is a wire-format change. Values whose low 32 bits are zero but high bits are not (e.g. 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z plus 1 tick) are written as timestamp32 with the truncated value (uint)data64 == 0, so the nanoseconds are silently lost. Nothing in the requirement asks for this.

Also round-trip new DateTime(1970,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc).AddTicks(1) through MessagePackSerializer on head: the deserialized value loses the tick (data corruption).

claim: The timestamp size check now masks the low 32 bits instead of the high 32 bits, which corrupts data and changes the wire format. If the low 32 bits of `data64` are zero (for example 1970-01-01T00:00:00.0000001Z, or 2106-02-07T06:28:16Z), the 6-byte timestamp32 form is used. It writes `(uint)data64`, which is 0, so the value deserializes as the Unix epoch and the nanoseconds and high seconds are lost. Every ordinary whole-second DateTime that used to encode as 6 bytes now encodes as 10-byte timestamp64.

claim: MessagePack attributes on the formatted type are never honoured. With no SurrogateType, the collector always uses CreateContractlessMembers, which emits string keys over all public read-write members. It ignores [MessagePackObject], [Key(int)] and [IgnoreMember] (and [DataContract]/[DataMember]) declared on T. So a referenced type with `[MessagePackObject]` and `[Key(0)]`/`[Key(1)]`/`[IgnoreMember]` gets a map-mode formatter that also serializes the ignored member. This contradicts the acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured'.

claim: The mask in the timestamp writer was changed from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. The timestamp32 branch (6 bytes) is now chosen when the low 32 bits are zero rather than when the high 32 bits are zero. Existing DateTime values will serialize as the wrong format and be corrupted. For example, a time with zero nanoseconds and seconds below 2^32 now falls into the 64-bit timestamp branch. Timestamp32 will be written for values with nonzero nanoseconds, which loses data. This change is unrelated to the requirement.

claim: The mask in the timestamp writer was changed from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. That inverts the timestamp32 vs timestamp64 selection. Timestamp32 is now chosen when the low 32 bits (seconds) are zero, not when the high 32 bits (nanoseconds and upper seconds) are zero. For a nonzero-seconds, zero-nanosecond DateTime, the encoder now takes the 8-byte timestamp64 path. For a DateTime with seconds==0 but nanoseconds>0, the 6-byte path is taken, which writes only the low 32 bits of data64, so the nanoseconds are silently dropped. The result is corrupted timestamps on serialization, and it is unrelated to this feature.
